text: The unexamined life is not worth living.
author: Socrates
notes: Said at his trial, when exile was offered in place of death. Socrates chose death over a life without **questioning** — for him, thinking about how to live *was* living.

text: Brevity is the soul of wit.
author: William Shakespeare
notes: Spoken by Polonius, one of the most long-winded characters in the play. The irony is the point.

text: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.
author: Jane Austen
notes:
The first sentence of *Pride and Prejudice* (1813), and one of the most quoted openings in English. It reads as a solemn general truth, then turns on its last words.

### The irony

The sentence claims that a rich single man must want a wife. The novel shows the opposite: it is the families of the neighbourhood who want the rich man, for one of their daughters. The "truth" is what the Bennets' world tells itself.

> However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered as the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters.

### Why it matters to the story

- The Bennets have five daughters and no son, so the family estate will pass to a cousin.
- Marriage is the only security open to the daughters, which makes the joke a serious one.
- Elizabeth refuses two proposals that would have solved the problem, and the book takes her side.

### Reading it again

Austen trusts the reader to hear two voices at once: the narrator's and the town's. Much of the novel's pleasure is in telling them apart. The whole text is free to read at [Project Gutenberg](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/1342).

text: Все счастливые семьи похожи друг на друга, каждая несчастливая семья несчастлива по-своему.
author: Лев Толстой
notes:
Первая фраза «Анны Карениной» (1878). Её часто цитируют как общий закон, хотя сам роман его проверяет и местами опровергает.

### О чём это

Счастье здесь описано как нечто общее и почти безличное, а несчастье — как то, что у каждой семьи своё. Сразу за этой фразой идёт: «Всё смешалось в доме Облонских», и роман начинается с конкретной беды.

- Семья Облонских: измена, которую прощают ради привычного порядка.
- Семья Карениных: брак, который рушится.
- Левин и Кити: долгий путь к счастью, которое оказывается вовсе не одинаковым.

Учёные даже назвали в честь этой фразы «принцип Анны Карениной»: успеху нужно, чтобы сошлось многое, а для неудачи достаточно одного.

text: Я помню чудное мгновенье: передо мной явилась ты
author: Александр Пушкин
孔子
notes: The opening line of the *Analects*: “Is it not a pleasure to learn, and to practise what you have learned?”

author: 老子
notes:
A journey of a thousand *li* begins beneath one's feet.

- Start where you stand.
- Keep walking.

text: 古池や蛙飛び込む水の音
author: 松尾芭蕉
notes: An old pond — a frog jumps in — the sound of water. See [the poem's history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_pond).

author: Delphic maxim
notes: “Know thyself”, inscribed in the forecourt of the Temple of Apollo at Delphi.

author: Arabic proverb
notes: Patience is the key to relief.

text: Carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero.
author: Horace
notes:
From Horace, *Odes* 1.11, written around 23 BC. The poem is addressed to a woman named Leuconoe, who is trying to learn the future from Babylonian astrology.

Horace tells her to stop: no one knows how many winters the gods will give. *Carpe* is a gardener's word, "pluck" rather than "seize", as one picks fruit when it is ripe. Trust tomorrow as little as you can.

text: Omnia, Lucili, aliena sunt, tempus tantum nostrum est.
author: Seneca
notes:
Everything else, Lucilius, belongs to others; only time is ours.

> Hold every hour in your grasp.
